---
title: "Grouped cross-validation"
---

The [cross-validation page](cross-validation.qmd) placed response rows into random folds. The same reader and story consequently occurred in both training and test data, so the held-out rows were not independent evaluations of new readers or stories. Recall that [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) concerns the joint data-generating model, not merely whether row indices differ. [**Grouped $K$-fold cross-validation**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data) instead assigns every row from a group to the same fold.

The [Natural Stories dossier](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories-measurement-dossier) fixed participant and story as two candidate grouping units. Holding out participants evaluates new readers of the represented stories. Holding out a story evaluates one omitted member of the ten construction-enriched texts.

We first construct folds that keep groups intact, then compare participant-held-out and story-held-out targets, return losses to the units receiving equal weight, and finally inspect leakage and the limits imposed by the available groups.

## Constructing grouped folds

Let $g(i)$ be the group containing observation $i$. Grouped validation requires

$$
g(i)=g(j)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{fold}(i)=\operatorname{fold}(j).
$$

The group controls both the split and the interpretation. Moving story rows together removes its sentences and word positions automatically; splitting sentences cannot evaluate an omitted story if other sentences from the same story remain in training.

## Participant and story validation targets {#participant-and-story-validation-targets}

The code fits the same population regression under two grouped designs. Their
[validation-target specifications](index.qmd#validation-target-specification) are:

| decision | participant design | story design |
|:--|:--|:--|
| split unit | participant | story |
| primary displayed score unit | computational fold | story |
| available information | lexical predictors and represented stories | lexical predictors and represented participants |
| refit inside fold | predictor moments and coefficients | predictor moments and coefficients |
| transfer target | similarly sampled readers of these stories | another omission among these ten enriched stories |

Participants receive one fixed five-fold assignment. Five is a computational compromise that
keeps about four fifths of the readers in each training fit. The shuffled round-robin
assignment balances participant counts to within one, but it is not type-balanced:
the prepared table supplies no participant stratum used by this algorithm. Stories
use leave-one-story-out validation because the scientific unit and the ten available
groups already define a complete rotation. Combining stories into five folds would
confound which omission produced a loss difference.

For the story comparison, a base model includes length and frequency, while an
expanded model adds GPT-3 surprisal. Each training fold estimates its own predictor
moments.

```{r}
#| label: natural-grouped-cv
#| message: false
#| warning: false

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
keep <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)
natural <- natural_all[keep, c(
  "participant_id", "story_id", "log_rt", "word_length",
  "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)]

make_group_folds <- function(group, folds, seed) {
  units <- sort(unique(as.character(group)))
  set.seed(seed)
  shuffled <- sample(units, length(units))
  assignment <- rep(seq_len(folds), length.out = length(shuffled))
  lookup <- setNames(assignment, shuffled)
  unname(lookup[as.character(group)])
}

participant_fold <- make_group_folds(
  natural$participant_id, folds = 5L, seed = 20261101
)
story_fold <- natural$story_id

stopifnot(all(tapply(
  participant_fold, natural$participant_id,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
) == 1))
stopifnot(all(tapply(
  story_fold, natural$story_id,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
) == 1))

cross_validated_prediction <- function(data, fold, predictors) {
  prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  for (current in sort(unique(fold))) {
    test <- fold == current
    train <- !test
    training_mean <- vapply(
      data[train, predictors, drop = FALSE], mean, numeric(1)
    )
    training_sd <- vapply(
      data[train, predictors, drop = FALSE], sd, numeric(1)
    )
    training_matrix <- sweep(
      as.matrix(data[train, predictors]), 2, training_mean, "-"
    )
    training_matrix <- sweep(training_matrix, 2, training_sd, "/")
    test_matrix <- sweep(
      as.matrix(data[test, predictors]), 2, training_mean, "-"
    )
    test_matrix <- sweep(test_matrix, 2, training_sd, "/")
    fit <- lm.fit(
      cbind("(Intercept)" = 1, training_matrix), data$log_rt[train]
    )
    prediction[test] <- drop(
      cbind("(Intercept)" = 1, test_matrix) %*% fit$coefficients
    )
  }
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(prediction)))
  prediction
}

base_predictors <- c("word_length", "log_unigram_frequency")
expanded_predictors <- c(base_predictors, "gpt3_surprisal")

participant_prediction <- cross_validated_prediction(
  natural, participant_fold, expanded_predictors
)
story_prediction <- cross_validated_prediction(
  natural, story_fold, expanded_predictors
)
story_base_prediction <- cross_validated_prediction(
  natural, story_fold, base_predictors
)

score_folds <- function(observed, prediction, fold, target) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(fold)), function(current) {
    rows <- fold == current
    error <- observed[rows] - prediction[rows]
    data.frame(
      target = target,
      fold = as.character(current),
      held_out_rows = sum(rows),
      rmse_log_rt = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
      mae_log_rt = mean(abs(error))
    )
  }))
}

grouped_scores <- rbind(
  score_folds(
    natural$log_rt, participant_prediction, participant_fold,
    "Participant"
  ),
  score_folds(
    natural$log_rt, story_prediction, story_fold,
    "Story"
  )
)

story_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  sort(unique(natural$story_id)),
  function(story) {
    rows <- natural$story_id == story
    base_error <- natural$log_rt[rows] - story_base_prediction[rows]
    expanded_error <- natural$log_rt[rows] - story_prediction[rows]
    data.frame(
      story_id = story,
      n_rows = sum(rows),
      base_rmse = sqrt(mean(base_error^2)),
      expanded_rmse = sqrt(mean(expanded_error^2)),
      base_minus_expanded_rmse =
        sqrt(mean(base_error^2)) - sqrt(mean(expanded_error^2))
    )
  }
))

grouped_scores
story_comparison

ggplot2::ggplot(
  grouped_scores,
  ggplot2::aes(target, rmse_log_rt)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0),
    size = 1.7,
      alpha = 0.75, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    color = "grey25"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Held-out unit",
    y = "Fold RMSE (log reading time)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  story_comparison,
  ggplot2::aes(factor(story_id), base_minus_expanded_rmse)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "#2B6CB0") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Held-out story",
    y = "RMSE reduction after adding GPT-3 surprisal"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

Participant-fold RMSE ranges from `r sprintf("%.4f", min(grouped_scores$rmse_log_rt[grouped_scores$target == "Participant"]))` to `r sprintf("%.4f", max(grouped_scores$rmse_log_rt[grouped_scores$target == "Participant"]))`. Story-fold RMSE ranges from `r sprintf("%.4f", min(grouped_scores$rmse_log_rt[grouped_scores$target == "Story"]))` to `r sprintf("%.4f", max(grouped_scores$rmse_log_rt[grouped_scores$target == "Story"]))`. These ranges should not be treated as a difficulty ranking because the held-out groups differ in size and composition. They show that predictive performance is a property of the validation target.

The plotted ranges are descriptive variation across these particular folds. They are
not [confidence intervals](../statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd): a confidence procedure calibrates random endpoints over repeated samples, whereas these endpoints are simply the minimum and maximum among the realized fold scores. Moreover, folds reuse training observations, participant folds are
arbitrary containers, and the ten story points exhaust the available enriched
stories rather than forming independent draws supplied by the validation algorithm.

Adding surprisal lowers leave-one-story-out RMSE for stories `r paste(story_comparison$story_id[story_comparison$base_minus_expanded_rmse > 0], collapse = ", ")` and raises it for stories `r paste(story_comparison$story_id[story_comparison$base_minus_expanded_rmse < 0], collapse = ", ")`. The changes range from `r sprintf("%.6f", min(story_comparison$base_minus_expanded_rmse))` to `r sprintf("%.6f", max(story_comparison$base_minus_expanded_rmse))` log-time units. Showing all story points prevents a pooled claim from concealing this heterogeneity.

## Group-weighted scores

For group $g$ with $n_g$ responses, define

$$
\overline L_g
=
\frac{1}{n_g}
\sum_{i:g(i)=g}L(y_i,\widehat y_i).
$$

A group-weighted score is

$$
\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^G\overline L_g.
$$

Each group receives equal weight. A row-weighted score instead pools all responses before averaging. The latter may be useful for corpus prediction, but its uncertainty cannot treat positions from one story as independent story transfers.

For a concrete unequal-size case, suppose Group A has one response with loss 9 and
Group B has nine responses, each with loss 1. The row-weighted loss is
$(9+9\times1)/10=1.8$. The group-weighted loss is
$[9+(9\times1)/9]/2=5$. Neither calculation is erroneous. The first targets a
random response row; the second targets a random group followed by a response within
that group.

## Group leakage and limits

Moving rows together does not prevent leakage from a response-derived predictor constructed before the split. A word-position mean reading time computed across all participants would contain the test participants' responses. For that reason, this analysis retains participant-level response rows and fits predictor transformations inside folds.

We keep the population regression and predictor set fixed while changing which empirical unit crosses the validation boundary. This restriction lets differences in loss reflect the participant-versus-story target rather than a simultaneous change in model structure. Reproducing the mixed-effects validation in Futrell et al. would require adding its group structure and refitting that complete procedure within every fold. The story results provide ten omissions among the released enriched texts; generalization to arbitrary English stories would require a sampling design and substantially more text-level replication.

## Checking the grouping variable

1. Why is a sentence split insufficient for an omitted-story target?
2. Which assertion verifies that participants do not cross folds?
3. Why can row-weighted and group-weighted losses answer different questions?
4. What does the story-difference plot show that a pooled RMSE change would hide?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Other sentences from the same story would remain in training.
2. The first `stopifnot()` checks that every participant has exactly one fold label.
3. Row weighting favors groups with more retained responses; group weighting gives
   every group equal influence.
4. It shows which particular story omissions improve or worsen after surprisal is
   added, rather than concealing that heterogeneity in one pooled score.

</details>

## Recap and forward link

1. The grouping variable determines which empirical unit is absent.
2. A computational fold and a score unit need not be the same object.
3. Row- and group-weighted losses target different sampling schemes.

The [previous page](cross-validation.qmd#the-validation-unit) evaluated new
rows from represented readers and stories. The [next page](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd#megaorientation-measurement-dossier)
switches to MegaOrientation and compares ordinal models on entirely unseen verbs.
